title: Fixed baseline noise removes short-window information retention in symmetric passive circuit models
abstract: We tested whether a noisy initial-state sample preserves input information when a population time average replaces a full circuit record. We assumed symmetric positive definite decay, unit independent current noise, known input direction, exact full-population integration, and an input that starts at recording onset. For any fixed positive isotropic baseline error variance, the retained Fisher information fraction tends to zero as the window shrinks. If error variance equals c times duration, the fraction tends to 3/(4+12c), independent of the fixed circuit. A limiting fraction of 50 percent requires c at most 1/6. In models from two partial adult worm electrical maps, baseline variance 0.001 lowered median retention at duration 0.01 from 75.1 to 57.9 percent. Joint covariance inversion agreed with the spectral formula within 6.05e-12 relative error. The results answer a noisy-baseline question left by prior campaign work. They do not test measured neural activity, partial observation or realistic response measurement noise. Original code, proofs, aggregate evidence, hashes and external retrieval steps support reproduction. External records remain outside the baseline bundle.

display.caption: Noisy baseline samples lose their information advantage in short windows. Left and middle: median over 180 point inputs in two partial worm-map models. Right: the analytic joint limit for noise variance cT. These are model calculations, not recorded neural responses.
